body.name: v0.2.0 (pre-release): optional persistent worker
body.body:
Unofficial community integration of [LeapTalk](https://github.com/zhangrongxiang/LeapTalk) for ComfyUI; not affiliated with the LeapTalk authors, Soul AI Lab, Meta or Comfy Org.

## New: optional persistent worker

Set `backend = persistent` on **LeapTalk Runtime** (or load `workflows/leaptalk_persistent.json`): the first job starts a worker that imports LeapTalk, loads the models and merges the LoRA once; later queue jobs reuse it. **LeapTalk Worker** shows the worker (`status`, never starts one, does not extend its idle time) or frees it (`unload`).

- **The worker keeps GPU and system memory while it is loaded**, also between jobs (on the test machine about 4 GiB of GPU memory and 8.4–8.8 GiB of Windows commit charge). It unloads after 120 s without a job (`worker_idle_seconds`), under memory pressure while idle, with Unload, and when ComfyUI exits.
- One-shot stays the default: v0.1 workflows and runtime configs run unchanged.
- A decoder, runtime or file change starts a new worker (the report says why); after any job error the worker is not reused; a failed persistent job never falls back to one-shot.
- Memory guard: a model load is refused at ≥ 90 % system commit or < 8 GiB available memory, a job when the projected commit would reach 97 %; a job and its worker are stopped when commit stays at or above 95 % for 5 s. Conservative defaults for the test machine, configurable per runtime (`memory_guard`).
- The worker is a local child process connected by pipes (no network port), placed in the same Windows job object as one-shot runs.

## Measured (RTX 5090, Windows 11, native runtime venv, ComfyUI v0.38.0 with `--cache-none`)

Queue to finished video through ComfyUI's HTTP API, median (range, runs):

| Speech | v0.1.0 one-shot | v0.2.0 one-shot | persistent, first job | persistent, warm jobs | frames |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 9.35 s | 36.1 s (31.8–40.4, 3) | 32.6 s (32.2–33.5, 3) | 30.4 s | **6.2 s** (5.8–8.2, 5) | identical in all runs, = official script |
| 33.98 s | 45.5 s (43.9–47.4, 3) | 45.3 s (44.0–46.6, 2) | 42.7 s | **17.7 s** (17.3–18.1, 5) | identical in all runs, = official script |

The runtime's output MP4s of the warm persistent jobs are byte-identical to the v0.1.0 release assets `leaptalk_a_short_9s.mp4` and `leaptalk_b_long_34s.mp4`. Ten different jobs on one worker (portraits A/B/A, speech changes, 0.5 s, silence, stereo 48 kHz) and a 96.5 s job (47 s) ran without state carried between jobs; LoRA merge and model load happened once per worker. Cancel, timeout, a missing model, a killed worker, a killed worker launcher, idle timeout, Unload, prompts queued at once and ComfyUI killed while idle or generating were tested on the GPU.

**Memory on the test machine:** a LeapTalk job (one-shot or persistent) peaks at about 16.5 GiB of Windows commit charge; with the desktop applications that were open, that is 94.5–95.5 % of the 93.3 GiB limit. With the default guard, warm Lite TAE jobs were refused or stopped when the background usage was slightly higher (including in the clean-install check, where the same workflows ran with `wan_vae`). Details: [docs/BENCHMARKS.md](https://github.com/hiroki-abe-58/ComfyUI-LeapTalk/blob/v0.2.0/docs/BENCHMARKS.md#persistent-worker).

## Tested / not tested

Tested with real weights: Windows 11 + native runtime venv (Python 3.12, torch 2.7.1+cu128), RTX 5090 32 GB, Lite TAE (and `wan_vae` as experimental), speech 0.5–96.5 s. CPU CI on Ubuntu and Windows (82 tests, including the worker protocol and lifecycle with a fake model). Not tested: Linux/other GPUs with real weights, non-English speech, speech longer than 96.5 s with real weights. Nobody has listened to the outputs (HUMAN_AUDIO_REVIEW_PENDING); lip sync was reviewed on frames only.

## Assets

- `leaptalk_v020_oneshot_vs_persistent_a_short_9s.mp4`: same portrait and speech, one-shot (left) vs warm persistent job (right), labelled with the measured times (new H.264 encode of two byte-identical outputs).
- `leaptalk_v020_persistent_a_short_9s.mp4`, `leaptalk_v020_persistent_b_long_34s.mp4`: outputs of warm persistent jobs.
- `run_manifest.json`: inputs (the v0.1.0 input assets), conditions, job evidence (prompt/job/worker/Engine ids, counters, frame hashes).
- `SHA256SUMS` (UTF-8, LF): `sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS`.

All media are AI-generated: fictional portraits (SDXL) and synthetic speech (Kokoro-82M); see docs/LICENSING.md. Use real faces and voices only with consent, and label generated media as AI-generated.

Comfy Registry: `leaptalk` 0.2.0 (review state in the registry; see the README).

---

### Clarification / known limitation (added 2026-10-03)

- The speed figures above are medians of the jobs that **completed** on one machine under its memory load at the time. 5.8x for the 9.35 s clip compares the v0.1.0 one-shot median (36.1 s) with the warm persistent median (6.2 s); against the v0.2.0 one-shot median (32.6 s) it is 5.2x.
- With a high Windows commit charge the memory guard refuses or stops **Lite TAE** jobs on a loaded worker. In the clean-install check of this release, 2 of 7 persistent Lite TAE jobs ran (the first job of each worker); the other 5 were refused before starting (projected commit 97.2-97.4 % against the 97 % limit). The clean-install series that passed used `decoder = wan_vae`: a different decoder (slower decoding, different frames), not a Lite TAE result.
- Loosening the guard is not the recommended fix. All attempts and outcomes: https://github.com/hiroki-abe-58/ComfyUI-LeapTalk/blob/main/docs/BENCHMARKS.md#all-attempts
- Unchanged: tag, source and assets of this release.

body.name: v0.1.0 (pre-release): portrait + speech -> talking video with the official LeapTalk recipe
body.body:
First release of an unofficial ComfyUI integration of [LeapTalk](https://github.com/zhangrongxiang/LeapTalk): **turn a portrait and speech into a talking video locally in ComfyUI.**

This is a **pre-release** because everything was verified on one machine: Windows 11, ComfyUI v0.38.0, a runtime venv on the same Windows machine, and an RTX 5090 32 GB.

**What it does**

- **LeapTalk Generate** takes one portrait (`IMAGE`) and one speech clip (`AUDIO`) and returns a 512x512, 25 fps `VIDEO` with the original audio, plus a JSON report.
- It uses the official LeapTalk recipe, which runs one solver step per chunk:
  - the SoulX-FlashHead-1_3B `Model_Pro` base;
  - the LeapTalk LoRA and audio projection (z-rx/leaptalk `b33b788`);
  - ViBT 1-step sampling with the Lite TAE decoder;
  - the LeapTalk code pinned at `5d8fef8`, unmodified.
- The LoRA (480/480 tensors) and the audio projection are verified on every job, and the generator calls are counted.
- The output is trimmed to `ceil(audio seconds x 25)` frames and muxed with your audio as AAC, without `-shortest`. The file is decoded back and checked.
- **LeapTalk Runtime** selects an administrator-registered runtime. **LeapTalk Doctor** checks a runtime without generating.

**Verified with real weights**

- **Same frames as the official `inference.py`**, through ComfyUI's Load Audio on a clean install:
  - 9.35 s clip: 234/234 frames identical;
  - 33.98 s clip: 850/850 frames identical.
- **Through ComfyUI's HTTP API**, from a `git archive` install in a differently named folder:
  - two fictional portraits, each with a ~10 s and a ~30 s speech clip;
  - the Wan VAE decoder and audio CFG 2.0;
  - stereo 48 kHz input, a 0.5 s clip, 3 s of silence and a 96.5 s clip;
  - Doctor;
  - cancel, timeout, a runtime error and a hard-killed ComfyUI: no runtime process was left and GPU memory returned to idle.
- **Wall time from queue to video** (each job loads the models, about 20 s, mostly Python imports):

  | Speech | Wall time |
  | --- | --- |
  | 9.4 s | 35 s |
  | 34 s | 43 s |
  | 96.5 s | 71 s |

  Once loaded, a 28-frame chunk takes about 0.43 s.
- **Memory**: the peak CUDA use was 8.1 / 11.1 GiB (allocated / reserved) with the Lite TAE and 6.1 / 7.6 GiB with the Wan VAE. On Windows, CUDA memory counted against the system commit charge.
- **Review**: frames were checked at word timings for all four portrait x speech combinations. The mouth moves from the first word, the last word is kept, and the mouth closes after the speech. Chunk boundaries show a small measurable step with no visible seam. This was not a listening test.

**Experimental / not verified**

- `decoder = wan_vae` works but is about 3x slower per chunk. It runs without `torch.compile`, while the official script compiles it.
- `audio_guidance` above 1: 2.0 gave visibly over-sharpened, discoloured lips.
- Not supported:
  - WSL2 runtimes (planned);
  - macOS (porting notes in docs/MACOS.md);
  - multi-GPU;
  - live streaming;
  - a persistent worker.
- Untested:
  - Linux hosts with real weights;
  - other GPUs;
  - flash-attn or SageAttention;
  - non-English speech.

**Assets** (all AI-generated, see docs/LICENSING.md)

| Asset | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| `leaptalk_a_short_9s.mp4`, `leaptalk_a_long_31s.mp4`, `leaptalk_b_short_10s.mp4`, `leaptalk_b_long_34s.mp4` | The four portrait x speech results of the release test. All four are published, none was picked out, and they are the runtime's own output with no editing. |
| `leaptalk_a_short_9s_wanvae.mp4` | The same input with the Wan VAE decoder. |
| `input_portrait_a.png`, `input_portrait_b.png` | Fictional adults generated with SDXL base 1.0. |
| `input_speech_*.wav` | Scripts written for this test, spoken by Kokoro-82M (synthetic voices). |
| `preview_a_short.gif` | A reduced, silent preview. |
| `run_manifest.json` | Prompts, seeds, scripts, model revisions, per-video frames, timings and hashes. |
| `SHA256SUMS` | Checksums of all assets. |

**Comfy Registry**: node id `leaptalk` (publisher `hiroki-abe-58`). Version 0.1.0 was uploaded from commit `86b9561`; the package holds 31 files and matches the commit byte for byte. At upload time it was waiting for the Registry's review (Pending). ComfyUI-Manager lists a version only after that review; until then, install from git as described in the README. The CDN package was installed by hand into a separate ComfyUI, where the Doctor (with sha256 checks) passed and a real generation succeeded.

**Checksums**: `SHA256SUMS` was written with Windows line endings. Use `SHA256SUMS.lf` with `sha256sum -c`; both list the same hashes.
